profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This CyrusOne cluster sits in the Cincinnati metro area, spanning Cincinnati, Lebanon, and Butler and Warren Counties in Ohio and Florence, Kentucky just across the Ohio River. This is CyrusOne home market: Wikipedia coverage states Cincinnati Bell purchased CyrusOne for 525 million dollars in 2010 and later divested its remaining stake in 2015 after the company IPO in 2013. CyrusOne was originally founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten. The company was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CyrusOne Lebanon, OH (CIN5) in Lebanon, Ohio, publishes 12 MW of IT capacity across 400,000 square feet of technical space, operated by CyrusOne.

At 10 kW per rack, a common enterprise colocation density, that load supports roughly 1200 racks. At 40 kW per rack, a density closer to AI training workloads, it supports roughly 300 racks. The operator has not published a per-rack power envelope, so neither figure is the operator's own claim, only what the published megawattage implies under each assumption.

CyrusOne Lebanon, OH (CIN5) holds 7 published certifications: SOC 2 Type 2 (audited controls over security, availability, and confidentiality, tested over time rather than at a point), PCI DSS (the standard required to handle payment card data), HIPAA (handling of protected health information), ISO 27001 (a certified information security management system), FISMA (a specific compliance or security standard), SSAE 16 Type II (a specific compliance or security standard). Together these qualify the facility for regulated workloads spanning security auditing, payments, and healthcare data, though which specific tenants rely on which certification is not disclosed.

Ohio has 5 facilities mapped in this site's dataset, of which 5 publish a megawatt figure, totaling 38.6 MW. CyrusOne Lebanon, OH (CIN5) contributes 12 MW of that total. At that published size it is a small facility relative to what frontier AI training infrastructure requires, which now runs into the tens or hundreds of megawatts, though it may still support inference workloads or smaller-scale AI applications.
